findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council remains under government commissioners' oversight with no autonomous borrowing authority
findings.detail: Following the May 2023 Department for Levelling Up Government Intervention decision and ongoing commissioners' oversight, all PWLB borrowing must be approved by both the Commissioners and MHCLG. The Capital Programme is reviewed annually by the s151 Officer and returned to PWLB/HM Treasury to confirm compliance with borrowing restrictions on investment assets purchased for yield.
findings.matters: Lenders should understand the council operates under statutory constraints with external governance oversight, limiting management autonomy in financial decision-making and borrowing strategy.
findings.figures: Government intervention period: 5 years (announced May 2023)
findings.quote: Following this intervention all PWLB borrowing needs to be agreed with the Commissioners and MHCLG.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Total borrowing increased to £2,185.4m despite debt reduction plan and asset disposals
findings.detail: The council's total borrowing increased from £2,155.6m at March 2025 to £2,185.4m at March 2026, an increase of £29.8m, despite the stated debt reduction plan and £22.7m in capital receipts from asset sales. This indicates that revenue funding deficits and capitalisation direction requirements have exceeded proceeds from asset disposals.
findings.matters: Net debt increase contradicts the narrative of debt reduction and suggests the restructuring has not yet achieved primary trajectory improvement. The CD usage for revenue is outpacing asset sale proceeds.
findings.figures: Borrowing: £2,185.4m (2026) vs £2,155.6m (2025); increase of £29.8m
findings.quote: The Council's borrowing and investment position at the beginning and end of the year is shown in the following table: [borrowing £2,185.4m vs £2,155.6m prior year]

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Revenue expenditure continues to be funded through Capitalisation Direction due to structural deficit
findings.detail: New borrowing in 2025/26 (beyond refinancing maturing loans) was primarily to support a Capitalisation Direction (special government borrowing approval) to fund revenue expenditure while the council works toward financial sustainability. A significant element of this CD relates to the loss of group company interest income. The use of capitalised borrowing to fund ongoing revenue indicates the council cannot balance its revenue budget from revenue sources alone.
findings.matters: This is a direct indicator of ongoing structural revenue deficit; the council remains dependent on special borrowing permissions to fund day-to-day expenditure, not just capital investment. This is the core condition that triggered the section 114 notice.
findings.figures: Capitalisation Direction used to fund revenue expenditure pending financial restructuring; £482.13m total borrowing in 2025/26
findings.quote: the primary reason for new borrowing in 2025/26, excluding the refinancing of loans maturing during the year, was to support the Capitalisation Directive (CD) required to fund revenue expenditure while the Council works towards a more sustainable financial position. A significant element of the CD relates to the loss of income following the suspension of interest previously received from wholly owned companies.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Capital receipt generation of £22.7m from commercial property portfolio disposals
findings.detail: The council generated £22.7m in capital receipts from General Fund asset disposals during 2025/26, reflecting ongoing disinvestment from its commercial property portfolio. These proceeds directly reduce the council's need to borrow and support debt reduction, embodying the core strategy to move out of commercial property holdings and reduce overall borrowing.
findings.matters: Asset disposals are the concrete operational activity supporting the stated debt reduction plan and disinvestment strategy. Lenders need to see whether this generates sufficient proceeds to materially improve debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £22.7 million in capital receipts from General Fund asset disposals
findings.quote: The Council has continued to make progress in delivering its debt reduction plan during 2025/26, generating £22.7 million of capital receipts from General Fund asset disposals. These disposals reflect the Council's ongoing strategy to disinvest from its commercial property portfolio and reduce its overall level of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Strategic shift to short-term one-year only borrowing, abandoning historic long-term annuity loans
findings.detail: The council took only 50 short-term one-year maturity loans in 2025/26 and no 50-year annuity loans, a fundamental change from its historic approach. This reflects a deliberate strategy shift due to: (1) treasury advisor recommendation to avoid locking in high interest rates, and (2) the council's decision to disinvest from property and group company holdings under an Asset Rationalisation Plan. One-year loans provide flexibility to repay debt as capital receipts materialise and avoid early repayment penalties on longer-term borrowing.
findings.matters: This signals the council's financial position and strategy: it cannot take long-term debt because it is actively divesting assets to reduce debt, not investing for the long term. It also indicates treasury advisors judge lasting improvement contingent on this restructuring.
findings.figures: Took 50 short-term loans at 4.26%–4.90%; zero long-term annuity loans
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council only took short-term borrowing over 1 year. This was due to two reasons; i. The Council's treasury advisors, MUFG (formerly called Link Group), recommended deferring long-term borrowing while interest rates were seen as high and were forecast to reduce... ii. The second reason was the change in the Council's strategic approach to Treasury Management... the Council is now disinvesting from its property and group company holdings. An Asset Rationalisation Plan is underway, under which the Council intends to dispose of most of its property portfolio and use the proceeds primarily to repay loan debt.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Interest income from group companies permanently suspended since section 114 notice
findings.detail: Interest receivable from wholly owned group companies has been suspended because the companies cannot fund payments following cessation of the council's revolving loan arrangements. This represents a permanent loss of revenue that was previously used to fund borrowing costs. The council is now implementing a 'debt sweep' arrangement where available surpluses are transferred back to offset lost interest, yielding £6.1m in 2025/26.
findings.matters: This is a structural loss of revenue that reduces the council's financial resilience and contributed to the need for the Capitalisation Direction to fund ongoing revenue expenditure.
findings.figures: £6.1m transferred from group companies in 2025/26 under debt sweep arrangement
findings.quote: The interest receivable from Group Companies has been suspended. The reason for the suspension is that the companies would be unable to fund the payments now that the Council's revolving loan arrangements with them have ended as part of the s114 notice in June 2023.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-035 Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: £500m government debt relief announced to address historic debt burden
findings.detail: In October 2025, the Government confirmed provision of an initial £500m debt relief package, described as 'a significant milestone in tackling Woking Borough Council's historic debt issue.' The detailed structure and timing remain subject to clarification, with officers still agreeing final terms with Government and commissioners.
findings.matters: This is a structural intervention that materially improves the council's debt position if it proceeds as intended, directly affecting financial sustainability and debt servicing burden.
findings.figures: £500 million initial tranche
findings.quote: In October 2025 the Government confirmed its intention to provide an initial tranche of £500 million of debt relief support. This is a significant milestone in tackling Woking Borough Council's historic debt issue.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-079 Future of ThamesWey Housing Limited (THL)
findings.headline: Disposal is part of Exceptional Financial Support recovery plan, indicating government intervention
findings.detail: This disposal is a key component of the Council's Improvement and Recovery Plan, indicating the council is operating under direct government oversight and Exceptional Financial Support due to financial distress.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the council is under direct government intervention and that failure to execute this disposal would represent breach of its recovery plan and could trigger further government action.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: It is also a key component of the Council's Company Divestment Strategy and debt reduction plan, which forms an essential part of the Council's Improvement and Recovery Plan.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-079 Future of ThamesWey Housing Limited (THL)
findings.headline: Disposal must complete by March 2027 under Local Government Reorganisation timescale, creating time pressure on complex transaction
findings.detail: The council must complete the acquisition, debt restructure, and disposal within nine months before being superseded by a unitary authority. This compressed timescale creates pressure to complete a complex multi-step transaction which could result in a lower sale price or weaker protections.
findings.matters: Time pressure on a distressed asset sale typically reduces proceeds and could result in the council failing to achieve its debt reduction targets or leaving difficult liabilities for the successor authority.
findings.figures: March 2027
findings.quote: The steps outlined in the report are intended to enable the corporate sale of THL to proceed with marketing and conclude the process prior to March 2027.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-079 Future of ThamesWey Housing Limited (THL)
findings.headline: 247 unprotected affordable homes could be converted to market rent, increasing homelessness costs
findings.detail: The portfolio includes 247 voluntary affordable homes with no legal protection. Unlike 335 Section 106-protected homes, these could be converted to market rent by a buyer, displacing vulnerable households and placing pressure on the council's temporary accommodation budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council faces potential future spending pressures on temporary accommodation if affordable housing protection is lost in the sale.
findings.figures: 247 voluntary affordable properties; 335 Section 106 protected; 768 market rent
findings.quote: It is also of relevance that any increase in rents post disposal is likely to result in the displacement of vulnerable households which will then place additional pressure on the Council's (and its successor's) resources concerning the provision of temporary accommodation for homelessness, expenditure in relation to which is already significant.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-079 Future of ThamesWey Housing Limited (THL)
findings.headline: Major subsidiary is balance sheet insolvent with £603m of unrecoverable council loans
findings.detail: ThamesWey Housing Limited owes the Council £603m through historical loans and rolled-up interest but is balance sheet insolvent, meaning the debt cannot be recovered. The council must eliminate this debt entirely through a debt-for-equity swap before the company can be sold, representing a material impairment of council assets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council is writing off a £603m loan against an asset that cannot generate returns, materially affecting financial position and the viability of the debt reduction strategy.
findings.figures: £603m as at 31st May
findings.quote: THL currently owes the Council £603m as at the 31st May, through historical loans and rolled up interest and, as a result, is balance sheet insolvent. This debt must be partially or wholly eliminated by the Council, to ensure that THL is solvent and that the shares are saleable.

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Company Divestment Strategy developed to exit unaffordable commercial commitments
findings.detail: A Company Divestment Strategy has been developed to release the Council from unaffordable commitments while optimizing asset value. The updated companies governance framework was approved in February 2026.
findings.matters: Councils exiting commercial ventures typically indicates those commitments were loss-making or unsustainable; this directly affects debt position and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Company Divestment Strategy 2025/26; governance framework approved February 2026
findings.quote: During 2025/26, a Company Divestment Strategy has been developed to support the delivery of this aim, whilst ensuring the Council takes account of wider social, economic and environmental impacts.

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council ceases to exist 1 April 2027; transition to West Surrey unitary authority creates operational uncertainty
findings.detail: Woking Borough Council will cease to exist on 1 April 2027 with establishment of West Surrey Council through Local Government Reorganisation. An internal LGR Co-ordination Group has been established to manage transition while maintaining service delivery.
findings.matters: The final year of operation creates uncertainty over debt obligations, service continuity during transition, and governance stability as institutions merge.
findings.figures: Vesting date 1 April 2027
findings.quote: On 1 April 2027, WBC will cease to exist, and West Surrey Council will be established. Maintaining robust governance arrangements will be critical for this transition.

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council operating under S114 notice issued 2023 with ongoing Government Commissioner oversight
findings.detail: Woking issued a Section 114 notice in 2023 triggering formal Government intervention. The Council operates under an Improvement and Recovery Plan overseen by Government Commissioners. The Commissioners' sixth report notes fundamental governance weaknesses leading to historic failings have been largely eliminated, but ongoing oversight continues.
findings.matters: Councils under S114 notice and active Government intervention present heightened financial and governance risk; continued Commissioner oversight indicates these remain active concerns.
findings.figures: S114 notice issued 2023; Government Commissioners overseeing IRP
findings.quote: the Financial Control Panel, in place since the Council's S114 notice was issued in 2023, continues to monitor all spend above £500 and is embedded into the organisation's processes.

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forensic review revealed governance failings; housing regulator involvement
findings.detail: Forvis Mazars undertook a forensic review of HRA historical transactions and financial arrangements, completed autumn 2025. The Council accepted all findings and implemented an action plan. Additionally, in March 2026 the Council self-referred to the Social Housing Regulator regarding an issue significantly impacting tenants.
findings.matters: HRA governance failures, combined with active Social Housing Regulator involvement, indicate service delivery and compliance risks in a material revenue-generating asset class.
findings.figures: Forensic review autumn 2025; Social Housing Regulator self-referral March 2026
findings.quote: an independent forensic review was commissioned during 2025 to look at historical transactions and financial arrangements concerning the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). Following a competitive tender process, Forvis Mazars were appointed and undertook the review, which was reported through Audit & Governance Committee, Executive & Full Council in Autumn 2025. The Council accepted the findings in full and has put in place an Action Plan

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Outstanding disclaimed audit opinions remain unresolved for multiple years
findings.detail: Six years of financial statements have been published but final audit opinions remain disclaimed. BDO's disclaimed opinions persist for years up to 2022/23 and Grant Thornton's for 2023/24 and 2024/25. Officers acknowledge this as a high priority but it remains outstanding.
findings.matters: Unresolved disclaimed audit opinions indicate unresolved governance and financial issues that undermine confidence in the council's accounts and control environment.
findings.figures: Disclaimed audit opinions outstanding for BDO (up to 2022/23) and Grant Thornton (2023/24-2024/25)
findings.quote: Final, disclaimed audit opinions remain outstanding from BDO up to 2022/23 and consequently Grant Thornton for the latter years, which officers continue to chase up as a high priority.

findings.paper_title: AUD26-016 Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Council still dependent on Exceptional Financial Support for debt despite first balanced operating budget
findings.detail: While Woking set a balanced business-as-usual budget for 2026/27 for the first time in years, Exceptional Financial Support continues to be required to cover overhanging debt and transformation costs. The Council is pursuing Asset Rationalisation and Debt Reduction Plans and is in active discussions with MHCLG on a longer-term solution to address debt levels.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council remains dependent on government support for debt servicing and that accumulated debt continues to require intervention.
findings.figures: Balanced BAU budget 2026/27; EFS continues for debt and transformation costs; Asset Rationalisation and Debt Reduction Plans active
findings.quote: Overall, in 2025/26 the Council made significant progress in strengthening the financial control environment, which culminated in the setting of a balanced 'business as usual' budget for 2026/27, meaning for the first time in many years that standard day-to-day services are fully funded, without reliance on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). EFS continues to be required to cover to the overhanging debt and transformation costs, and new business-as-usual savings will continue to be sought for future years. The Council is progressing its Asset Rationalisation and Debt Reduction Plans to mitigate this, alongside discussions with MHCLG on a longer-term solution.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-032 Budget Monitoring Draft Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: The General Fund cannot balance without £171.1m in exceptional financial support from government
findings.detail: The entire budget is dependent on £171.1m of exceptional support: £96.5m deferred Minimum Revenue Provision and £74.6m Capitalisation Directive. Without this government support, the budget would not balance, indicating structural revenue shortfall.
findings.matters: Structural reliance on deferred MRP and capitalisation directives indicates the council cannot operate on its core revenue base; future years depend on continued government support which is uncertain and temporary.
findings.figures: £171.1m exceptional financial support (£96.5m MRP deferral + £74.6m Capitalisation Directive); provisional outturn variance £15.0m
findings.quote: The Council's 2025/26 General Fund revenue budget was underpinned by £171.1m Exceptional Financial Support from government, consisting of a £96.5m deferral of Minimum Revenue Provision and £74.6m provisional Capitalisation Direction, which itself is underpinned by further borrowing.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-032 Budget Monitoring Draft Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: The £15m favorable outturn is primarily from non-recurring items: £6.1m subsidiary cash sweeps and £6.0m treasury gains
findings.detail: The headline favorable variance comprises £6.1m unbudgeted cash sweeps from subsidiary companies, £6.0m treasury management gains from lower interest rates, and only £2.9m from operational service underspends. The favorable position does not represent underlying operational improvement.
findings.matters: Non-recurring items cannot be relied upon for future years; the underlying operational position is much tighter than the headline variance suggests, masking structural budget pressure.
findings.figures: £6.1m cash sweeps (non-recurring), £6.0m treasury gains (non-recurring), £2.9m service underspends
findings.quote: £6.1m unbudgeted income received from cash sweeps from Thameswey Group and VSWL under the agreed Debt Standstill agreements.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-032 Budget Monitoring Draft Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council is setting aside £1.3m now because it expects a Business Rates collection fund deficit in 2027-28
findings.detail: The council has explicitly identified and reserved for a known upcoming shortfall in Business Rates collection for 2027-28. This pre-emptive reserve creation confirms the deficit is anticipated and measurable.
findings.matters: Collection fund deficits must be funded from council reserves or budget; this will create a claim on resources in 2027-28 and crowds out discretionary spending.
findings.figures: £1.3m Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve for 2027-28 Business Rates Collection Account deficit
findings.quote: £1.3m to the Collection Fund Equalisation Reserve, ensuring funding is set aside to mitigate a known upcoming deficit on the Business Rates Collection Account in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-032 Budget Monitoring Draft Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Council has set aside £7m specifically for risks in its commercial portfolio, including Thameswey Energy Limited
findings.detail: The council identified material commercial sector risks significant enough to create a dedicated £7m reserve. This explicit provision signals management concern about potential losses in commercial investments, specifically naming Thameswey Energy as a risk.
findings.matters: Commercial portfolio losses could erode reserves and impair the council's financial position; the reserve size indicates expected potential losses are material relative to core operations.
findings.figures: £7.0m Commercial Risks Reserve; council holds stakes in Thameswey Group and VSWL
findings.quote: £7.0m to a Commercial Risks Reserve to manage risks associated with the Council's commercial portfolio, including Thameswey Energy Limited.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-032 Budget Monitoring Draft Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: Woking is under formal Government Commissioner oversight with an ongoing Improvement & Recovery Plan
findings.detail: The council is supervised by Government Commissioners who are receiving regular progress reports on financial recovery. Section 8.2 confirms the council is managing an Improvement & Recovery Plan with Commissioners oversight, indicating the council was in prior financial stress and remains under formal management.
findings.matters: Government intervention signals prior or present financial stress and ongoing regulatory scrutiny; it materially affects the risk profile for any potential lender or credit decision.
findings.figures: £2.52m spent on Improvement & Recovery Programme in 2025-26; Commissioners sixth report to MHCLG referenced
findings.quote: Government Commissioners have been consulted on the proposals within this report.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Limited historical due diligence on property acquisitions and poor understanding of hold costs has contributed to £247m portfolio with insufficient returns
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that when commercial investments were made, there was limited due diligence and poor understanding of hold costs versus financial returns. A new asset management system has been implemented since intervention, and a three-year divestment programme is underway with external advisors.
findings.matters: Governance failure contributed to the current crisis. This documents both the root cause and the remediation, but demonstrates the scale of management breakdown that occurred.
findings.figures: £247m commercial property portfolio; three-year divestment programme underway
findings.quote: Historically there has been limited due diligence on land and property acquisitions and a poor understanding of their hold costs versus the financial return.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Debt standstill extended for 2026/27 contingent on companies remaining operationally solvent and meeting government conditions
findings.detail: A further debt standstill with Thameswey and Victoria Square will be considered by Council on 12 February 2026. The standstill is contingent on companies maintaining positive EBITDA, demonstrating cash solvency, submitting approved business plans, and meeting subsidy control tests. Costs of suspended interest and MRP are expected to be addressed by a Capitalisation Direction to be confirmed in February/March 2026.
findings.matters: The standstill is a critical near-term decision point. Failure to meet conditions could force administration of the companies, crystallising losses.
findings.figures: Debt standstill decision 12 February 2026; cash sweep payments totalled £6.1m from April–December 2025
findings.quote: a further debt standstill with the Thameswey and Victoria Square Woking Limited groups of companies will be considered by Council on 12 February 2026... The debt standstill is subject to the companies meeting the following tests

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Cladding failure on Victoria Square Woking hotel may have material impact on asset divestment values
findings.detail: The document flags that cladding remediation works on the hotel and the need to improve commercial management of energy companies represent issues that 'may have a potentially material impact on divestment values'. Capital work is substantively complete but debt continues to accrue, creating urgency to divest at pace.
findings.matters: A concrete near-term liability has emerged that could reduce proceeds from the planned three-year asset disposal programme, on which the debt reduction strategy depends.
findings.figures: Capital work on Sheerwater and Victoria Square schemes substantively complete; debt accruing during divestment
findings.quote: Issues which may have a potentially material impact on divestment values include the recent cladding failure on the Victoria Square Woking Limited hotel and the need to improve commercial management of the energy companies.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Share investments impaired from £37.8m to £4.8m in 2024/25 accounts
findings.detail: The council's shareholdings in subsidiaries and local businesses were written down by £33m (87% impairment) in the 2024/25 accounts, reflecting the balance sheet insolvency of underlying companies.
findings.matters: Confirms the depth of loss on the council's investment portfolio and the poor quality of asset valuations.
findings.figures: Share investments impaired from £37.8m to £4.8m
findings.quote: the Council's share investments were impaired from £37.8m to £4.8m.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio rental income is insufficient to service financing and holding costs, hitting the General Fund
findings.detail: The £247m commercial property portfolio (balance sheet valuation) generates rental income that does not cover borrowing costs and operational expenses. The operational impact of managing voids and landlord costs (service charges, business rates) has had a significant impact on the General Fund.
findings.matters: A major asset class is income-negative on a cash basis, meaning it drains rather than supports the General Fund budget.
findings.figures: £247m commercial property portfolio valuation; net income from strategic property portfolio £6m (before staffing and financing costs)
findings.quote: Whilst the assets contribute rental income to the Council's budget, this is currently insufficient to service financing and holding costs. The operational impact of managing the loss of income from voids alongside the associated increase in costs to the landlord (the Council) for service charges and business rates has had a significant impact on the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Thameswey and Victoria Square Woking Limited are balance sheet insolvent with insufficient EBITDA to service £46m annual interest
findings.detail: Both company groups' latest audited accounts confirm balance sheet insolvency with asset values materially below liabilities. Though the companies are EBITDA-positive operationally, they do not earn enough to service full interest and principal liabilities. Interest payments of £46m per annum are currently suspended.
findings.matters: The council's largest commercial holdings are insolvent and dependent on debt standstill arrangements. Interest suspension represents a hidden subsidy and revenue-account exposure.
findings.figures: £46m annual interest from Thameswey and Victoria Square; Thameswey group fixed assets £473m; Victoria Square fixed assets £134m; both balance sheet insolvent
findings.quote: The latest audited accounts for the Thameswey group of companies (company number 03702545) and Victoria Square Woking Limited (company number 08005542) confirm that the companies are balance sheet insolvent... The interest due to the Council from the Thameswey group of companies and Victoria Square Woking Limited is c£46 million per annum.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: General Fund structural deficit persists even if all commercial assets are fully disposed of
findings.detail: The debt model supporting the Medium Term Financial Plan shows that even complete disposal of all commercial investments and property would not eliminate the structural deficit. The deficit is largely driven by debt interest and Minimum Revenue Provision charges on the remaining debt.
findings.matters: This indicates the council faces a fundamental structural imbalance that cannot be solved through asset sales; ongoing government support or service reductions are inevitable.
findings.figures: Structural deficit persists despite modelled full asset disposal
findings.quote: The model shows that, without a long term solution to the high level of debt, and even if all commercial assets (including the commercial property portfolio and company holdings) were fully disposed of, the General Fund would continue to face a significant structural deficit largely driven by debt interest and Minimum Revenue Provision costs.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: £1.2–1.4bn of the council's debt is not backed by realisable assets, limiting capacity to reduce borrowing through asset sales
findings.detail: The Section 114 notice identified that asset values materially lag loan balances. This unsecured debt cannot be reduced through the planned three-year divestment programme, creating a structural gap that requires either debt relief or long-term government support.
findings.matters: Asset sales, which are the council's primary debt reduction mechanism, cannot address the majority of the debt burden, making the council's financial position dependent on continued government intervention.
findings.figures: £1.2bn–£1.4bn of debt unmatched by realisable assets
findings.quote: It is estimated that between £1.2 billion and £1.4 billion of the Council's debt is not backed by realisable assets.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: £663m impairment of company loans identified in 2024/25 accounts following Section 114 notice
findings.detail: The May 2023 External Assurance Review concluded that the council's historic investment decisions were disproportionate to its resources and lacked commercial skills. The resulting Section 114 notice found unaffordable borrowing, inadequate MRP provision, and significant shortfall between asset values and loans advanced. Company loans were impaired by £663m in the 2024/25 accounts, plus a further £155m for loans found to be for revenue purposes contrary to regulations.
findings.matters: This represents historic regulatory breach and governance failure, with £155m of borrowing used for revenue purposes in violation of statutory requirements.
findings.figures: £663m impairment of company loans; £155m additional impairment for revenue-purpose loans
findings.quote: the company loans have been impaired by £663 million in the Council's 2024/25 Accounts along with the further impairment of £155 million for loans assumed to be used for revenue purposes... the company loans have been impaired by £663 million in the Council's 2024/25 Accounts

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Woking has the highest debt per head of population of any local authority in the UK and requires ongoing government Exceptional Financial Support despite £500m debt relief
findings.detail: The council holds £1.8bn in investments funded primarily by borrowing, with debt substantially exceeding asset values. Even with the committed £500m government debt relief reducing borrowing to around £1.7bn, the associated interest and Minimum Revenue Provision charges remain unaffordable, and the council will still require Exceptional Financial Support in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This is an unprecedented position for a UK local authority, indicating structural insolvency that cannot be resolved through normal budget management or asset sales alone.
findings.figures: £1.8bn total investments; £1.7bn debt after £500m relief; debt model shows structural deficit persists even with complete asset disposal
findings.quote: The Council currently has the highest debt per head of population of any local authority in the UK with total group investments of c£1.8 billion... the Council requires Exceptional Financial Support from government to be able to set its annual budget and Council Tax.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Banking facilities are essential to funding plans and at risk due to Section 114 notice
findings.detail: Lloyds Bank has a policy requiring councils with Section 114 notices to have their banking facilities reviewed. The document acknowledges that banking facilities are essential to the council's current funding plans but must be subject to executive review in light of the Section 114 status.
findings.matters: This indicates the council's day-to-day banking and cash management facilities are contingent on bank policy review. Loss of banking facilities would impair the council's ability to operate and manage cash flows.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Lloyds, have a policy for Councils subject to a Section114 notice that requires the Executive to consider the Council's continued use of facilities which it has with Lloyds Bank in light of the issue of the Section 114 notice.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Council cannot set a lawful budget without exceptional MRP relief from government
findings.detail: The strategy confirms that the council has requested exceptional MRP relief (deferring £92m of MRP charge) as part of its Exceptional Financial Support application, and states this relief is required 'to enable the Council to set a lawful budget for 2026/27'. This means without government approval, the council cannot balance its budget.
findings.matters: This indicates the council's financial position is dependent on continued government discretion. It shows the council cannot independently set a lawful budget, placing it at risk if government support is withdrawn or restricted.
findings.figures: £92m MRP deferral requested; business-as-usual MRP charge £1.045 million
findings.quote: This exceptional MRP relief, if approved, would enable the Council to set a lawful budget for 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Large debt maturity wall: £357 million of borrowing matures in 2026/27 requiring immediate refinancing
findings.detail: The council must refinance £357m of maturing loans in 2026/27, plus £87m of new borrowing for the capital programme and capitalisation directive. This creates significant refinancing risk and exposure to interest rate changes, particularly as the council can only borrow from PWLB subject to regular government approval.
findings.matters: This large concentration of maturing debt in a single year creates refinancing risk. It also ties the council's borrowing strategy to government decisions, limiting flexibility.
findings.figures: £357 million maturing in 2026/27; total borrowing requirement £444 million including £87m forecast increase in gross loan debt
findings.quote: £357 million of the Council's existing borrowing matures in 2026/27, and this will need to be reborrowed

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Government's £500m debt support is insufficient; further support expected to be required
findings.detail: The strategy document states that even after the committed £500m debt support, the council will be unable to meet all remaining borrowing liabilities and associated debt costs. Officers are continuing to work with government on finding a long-term solution, indicating further extraordinary support is anticipated.
findings.matters: This indicates the £500m support is a partial solution only. The council is signalling to lenders that it expects to require additional government bailout. The timing and amount of any further support is unknown.
findings.figures: £500 million committed; payment date and mechanism not yet confirmed
findings.quote: further support is expected to be required in future, as the Council is unable to meet all remaining borrowing liabilities and associated debt‑charge costs.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Interest burden is unaffordable even with the £500m government debt support
findings.detail: The council's budget shows gross interest payable of £68.6m in 2026/27, with general fund financing costs of £63.0m after interest receivable. The document explicitly states this interest burden is unsustainable even with government support, indicating the debt support is insufficient to resolve the underlying problem.
findings.matters: This signals that the council's debt burden cannot be managed within its revenue base, even with substantial government support. It suggests further extraordinary measures or support will be required.
findings.figures: Gross interest payable 2026/27: £68,572k; General Fund gross financing costs: £63,651k
findings.quote: this interest burden is far higher than the Council is able to sustain even with the £500m debt support confirmed by Government.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Unaffordable MRP charge: the council systematically understated minimum revenue provision for years by not charging on company loans
findings.detail: An independent review found the council significantly understated MRP by policy (not charging on loans to companies). Backlog MRP totalled £406.5m in previous support packages. For 2026/27, the council has requested another £92m of MRP be deferred through exceptional financial support; without this, it cannot set a lawful budget.
findings.matters: This is a material accounting failure spanning multiple years. It means the council's historical accounts understated its liabilities. The continued need for MRP relief shows the underlying problem is not solved.
findings.figures: Backlog MRP £406.5 million; 2026/27 MRP deferral requested £92 million; proposed business-as-usual charge only £1.045 million
findings.quote: This review confirmed the Council, due predominantly to the policy of not charging MRP on the loans to companies, has systematically understated its MRP. Backlog MRP included in previous Exceptional Financial Support packages totalled £406.5 million.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Failed investments in commercial companies created the debt crisis and suspended all interest income to the council
findings.detail: The council relied on high-value commercial company investments to fund its borrowing costs, but these failed. As a result, the council has lost all interest revenue from the companies and is dependent on government support to cover the resulting revenue gap. The paper identifies this as the core cause of the Section 114 notice issued in June 2023.
findings.matters: This reveals the root cause of the financial distress: a failed corporate investment strategy, not operational overspend. It shows material governance failure in approving unsustainable debt-funded investments.
findings.figures: Interest income from ThamesWey and VSWL budgeted at £0 in 2026/27 (previously funded part of borrowing costs)
findings.quote: The Council's financial difficulties (underpinning the issuing of a Section 114 notice in June 2023) relate to the extremely high level of the Council's loan debt combined with the Council's reliance on failed high value investments in the commercial companies to fund the borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft) Council March 2026 Revised
findings.headline: Council decisions on debt reduction are overseen by Commissioners and dependent on government approval
findings.detail: Multiple paragraphs reference ongoing discussions between officers, Commissioners, and government on the timing and nature of financial support. This indicates the council is operating under some form of government intervention or recovery regime where major financial decisions require external approval.
findings.matters: Commissioner oversight signals regulatory intervention and reduced autonomy over financial decision-making. This increases governance risk for lenders.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Discussions between officers, the Commissioners and government on the nature, quantum and timing of support are ongoing and depend on the Council's ongoing work on asset disposals and service efficiencies.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft) Council March 2026 Revised
findings.headline: PWLB loan repayment is discouraged by embedded premiums, requiring government intervention on loan terms
findings.detail: The council notes that premiums (or discounts) on PWLB loans act as a disincentive to early repayment of debt. The council is in discussions with government to review these arrangements to facilitate a debt repayment programme. This suggests the council is locked into expensive PWLB debt with significant early repayment penalties.
findings.matters: Embedded PWLB premiums limit the council's ability to reduce debt efficiently and indicate underlying constraints on the council's financial flexibility. This is a structural problem requiring government-level intervention.
findings.figures: Unspecified premium amounts
findings.quote: The premium (or discount) payment required on PWLB loans will be calculated as part of any debt charge savings as it can be a disincentive to actual debt repayment so this should NOT be used in a decision on sale (i.e. as a reason for not selling). Discussions are underway with government on how a programme of repayment can be facilitated by reviewing these arrangements for the Council.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft) Council March 2026 Revised
findings.headline: Council is disposing of most or all of its commercial investment portfolio to reduce debt
findings.detail: The council's investment portfolio is under comprehensive review with a view to disposing of most or all holdings. This is described as a major part of the council's Improvement and Recovery Plan's commercial workstream. Proceeds will be applied to debt reduction, signalling the council is liquidating assets to reduce borrowing.
findings.matters: Large-scale asset disposal reduces the council's revenue-generating capacity and signals financial distress. Lenders need to understand the impact on future revenue streams and the council's ability to fund services.
findings.figures: Unspecified quantum of commercial portfolio
findings.quote: The Council's investment portfolio is currently under comprehensive review with a view to disposing of most or all of them in order to reduce the Council's debt. This is a major part of the Improvement and Recovery Plan's Commercial workstream

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft) Council March 2026 Revised
findings.headline: Government debt support of £500 million is conditional on progress with asset disposal plan
findings.detail: The council has secured a commitment from government to provide £500 million in debt support for 2026-27, but this is explicitly contingent on demonstrable progress with the asset rationalisation plan. This creates a dependency where the council must meet asset sale targets to access the support it needs to balance its accounts.
findings.matters: Conditional support is riskier than unconditional support. Failure to meet asset disposal targets could leave the council unable to access the funding it is counting on, creating a cliff-edge risk.
findings.figures: £500 million debt support committed
findings.quote: Government have committed to £500 million debt support in 2026/27 subject to progress with the asset rationalisation plan.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft) Council March 2026 Revised
findings.headline: Estimated MRP of £95 million is unaffordable and cannot be met in full by the council
findings.detail: The calculated 2026-27 Minimum Revenue Provision is £95 million, but the council can only afford to provide £1.042 million on a business-as-usual basis (down from £8 million in 2025-26). The remaining ~£93.96 million must be deferred through a request for government Exceptional Financial Support. This represents a critical affordability gap in the council's debt servicing.
findings.matters: MRP is a statutory obligation to set aside money for debt repayment. An unaffordable MRP signals the council cannot service its debt from its own resources and is dependent on exceptional government intervention.
findings.figures: £95 million calculated MRP; £1.042 million affordable provision (2026/27); £8 million (2025/26); £500 million government debt support committed (conditional)
findings.quote: The Council's estimated MRP for 2026/27 – calculated based on the policy above - is £95 million. The Council's 2026/27 MRP as calculated is unaffordable and cannot be met in full by the Council.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Council may still discover additional financial issues relating to past practice and financial systems
findings.detail: The CFO acknowledges that there is still potential to discover new financial issues relating to past practice, financial systems, and management reporting. This reflects ongoing work to improve financial information quality and a system upgrade planned for 2025/26. The pattern suggests additional issues may continue to emerge.
findings.matters: The acknowledgment of unknown liabilities creates uncertainty about the true baseline financial position and risk of further pressures emerging in 2026/27.
findings.figures: System upgrade planned 2025/26; impact figures not specified
findings.quote: There is still potential that the Council could discover new financial issues relating to past practice, both generally and with regards to its financial systems and the management reporting from them.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Waste services contract dispute with risk of unfavourable outcome requiring emergency funding
findings.detail: The council is involved in a contract dispute with its waste supplier. Resources are set aside in 2026/27, but an unfavourable outcome could create further financial pressures. Additionally, waste re-tendering from June 2027 carries risk that bids could exceed budget assumptions.
findings.matters: A specific contingent liability exists that could require emergency funding at a time when the council has minimal financial flexibility and is already stretched.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Service budget overspends reported at Q3 2025/26 with ongoing pressures in homelessness, parking and finance function
findings.detail: Q3 2025/26 monitoring shows c.£1m overspend on service and savings budgets. Key pressures include parking maintenance costs and income targets; homelessness and temporary accommodation demand and costs; and finance reliance on interim resource. The CFO notes some pressures will continue into 2026/27 requiring mitigation.
findings.matters: Current-year overspends indicate the council is struggling to maintain spending discipline despite monitoring improvements, with demand-led pressures it cannot control.
findings.figures: c.£1m overspend at Q3 2025/26
findings.quote: Budget monitoring at Q3 reports a c.£1m overspend on service and savings delivery budgets offset by underspends on treasury management.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Reliance on £323m asset disposal pipeline in 2026/27 to meet government conditions and reduce debt
findings.detail: Asset Rationalisation and Debt Reduction Plans project asset disposals of c.£323m in 2026/27. This is a condition of Exceptional Financial Support. The council must achieve best consideration and maximise receipts. However, risks identified include property voids, unforeseen capital/maintenance works, and property portfolio risks.
findings.matters: Council's ability to maintain government support depends on executing a £323m disposal programme. Failure would likely trigger renegotiation of support terms and reveal further unsustainability.
findings.figures: c.£323m asset disposal pipeline for 2026/27
findings.quote: The Council continues to pursue its Asset Rationalisation and Debt Reduction Plans, which project an asset disposal pipeline of c.£323m in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Interest costs of £62.6m in 2026/27, with additional cost risk if £500m government support is delayed beyond mid-year
findings.detail: Interest costs are projected at £62.6m for 2026/27. The budget assumes £500m government debt support will be delivered by the mid-point of 2026/27. If delays occur, the council would incur additional interest costs beyond budget in a year with very limited financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Interest costs consuming this proportion of a £21m core spending power indicate severe financial stress, with additional exposure to government payment delays.
findings.figures: £62.6m interest costs projected 2026/27; £500m government support subject to timing risk
findings.quote: The associated interest costs are projected at £62.6m in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: £92.1m Minimum Revenue Provision deferred for 2026/27, meaning debt is not being repaid
findings.detail: The council is deferring £92.1m in MRP for 2026/27 relating to historic debt. This deferral is permitted under government statutory MRP guidance for intervened authorities, but means the council is not making debt repayment provisions as would normally be required under the Prudential Code.
findings.matters: MRP deferral means debt repayment is suspended, with the council relying entirely on government support and asset sales rather than genuine debt service capacity.
findings.figures: £92.1m MRP deferred for 2026/27
findings.quote: The 2026/27 Exceptional Financial Support package requests approval to continue to defer MRP totalling £92.1m for 2026/27 related to historic debt.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Government support is interim with no long-term solution identified; Local Government Reorganisation by April 2027 adds uncertainty
findings.detail: The council describes current Exceptional Financial Support as 'interim finance support arrangement, pending further discussions with Government'. No sustainable long-term solution has been reached despite nearly three years of intervention. Local Government Reorganisation is due April 2027, meaning financial planning work will continue beyond the new unitary council's vesting day.
findings.matters: Interim support with no long-term plan and concurrent local government reorganisation create ongoing uncertainty about the council's financial stability beyond 2026/27.
findings.figures: LGR implementation 1 April 2027; £1m budget provision for LGR workstreams in 2026/27
findings.quote: It is important to note that for the reasons outlined above this remains an interim finance support arrangement, pending further discussions with Government to reach a way forward that addresses the issues outlined above.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: CFO explicitly states council remains financially unsustainable despite balanced 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The Chief Finance Officer states that despite preparing a balanced business-as-usual budget for 2026/27, the council 'remains in a financially unsustainable position' due to legacy debt. Long-term financial sustainability has not been achieved and the council is dependent on government support and asset disposals.
findings.matters: The statutory financial officer is confirming the council cannot sustain itself without continued external intervention, indicating structural financial failure.
findings.figures: Budget is balanced for 2026/27 only; sustainability forecast to 2028/29 remains uncertain
findings.quote: Despite preparing a balanced business-as-usual budget for 2026/27, due principally to the legacy debt the Council remains in a financially unsustainable position

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 3 - Section 25 Statement and Risk Assessment
findings.headline: Outstanding debt of £2.2bn with asset values materially less than debt, even after £500m government support
findings.detail: The council issued a Section 114 notice in June 2023 due to understatement of Minimum Revenue Provision, loans to companies for revenue purposes, and understated repairs budgets. Core spending power is only £21m in 2026/27 while outstanding debt stands at c.£2.2bn. Despite £500m government support, the value of associated assets is materially less than the debt owed.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council's asset base is insufficient to cover debt obligations, creating substantial credit risk with limited recovery value.
findings.figures: £2.2bn outstanding debt; £500m government support; £21m Core Spending Power; £62.6m interest costs 2026/27
findings.quote: The level of outstanding debt is c.£2.2bn, and even with the provision of £500m government support, the value of the associated assets is materially less than the debt.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Business rates income guarantee reduces from 100% to 92.5% by 2028/29, creating exposure to economic decline risk
findings.detail: Government has guaranteed councils will receive 100% of their assessed baseline funding need from business rates in 2026/27. However, this guarantee reduces to 97% in 2027/28 and drops to 92.5% from 2028/29 onwards. If business rates decline in Woking's area due to economic conditions, the council will be exposed to unprotected losses of up to 7.5% of collectible rates from 2028/29.
findings.matters: Business rates are a key revenue source (£2.5m forecast retained for 2026/27). Declining guarantees combined with potential economic slowdown or recession create material downside risk to income projections, particularly from 2028/29 when guarantee protection is lowest.
findings.figures: 100% guarantee 2026/27; 97% guarantee 2027/28; 92.5% guarantee 2028/29+; £2.5m retained business rates forecast
findings.quote: However, in future years the guarantee will reduce to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% in 2028/29, meaning if business rates decline in a particular area, the local authority will be exposed to losses of up to 3% in 2027/28 and 7.5% from 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Current-year revenue overspends of £1m in 2025/26 indicate service control issues persist despite intervention regime
findings.detail: Quarter 3 monitoring for the current 2025/26 financial year reports net forecast overspends of £1m across services. The paper acknowledges that while these can be covered by treasury management gains this year, work must continue into 2026/27 to 'mitigate service spending to contain it within the agreed budget envelope.' This suggests underlying service budget management weaknesses persist despite government intervention and Commissioner oversight.
findings.matters: A council under Section 114 notice with Commissioners in place should demonstrate tight spending discipline. Current-year overspends, even if covered, indicate the control framework is not yet fully effective. This raises questions about whether optimistic 2026/27 budget assumptions will hold in practice.
findings.figures: £1m net forecast service overspends in 2025/26
findings.quote: additional challenges arise from the net forecast overspends across services of c.£1m in the current year 2025/26

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Structural budget deficit of £5.5m forecast from 2027/28 when £3m annual Victoria Gate lease income terminates
findings.detail: The 2026/27 business-as-usual (BAU) budget is balanced at £22.0m, but this masks a cliff edge. The £3m annual lease premium income from the Victoria Gate development is due to end, triggering a forecast BAU deficit of £5.5m in 2027/28 rising to £6.7m in 2028/29. The council has identified this but indicated it will be difficult to close without further government support or significant service reductions, given its existing difficulty achieving net savings.
findings.matters: The 2026/27 budget balance is temporary and dependent on a single income stream. The imminent cliff edge (2027/28) will likely require another government support request before the recovery plan is complete. This extends the council's dependency period and tail risk.
findings.figures: £3m annual Victoria Gate lease income ending; £5.5m BAU deficit 2027/28; £6.7m BAU deficit 2028/29
findings.quote: the Council's projected BAU budget gap on day-to-day services for 2026/27 was estimated at £0.7m, but forecast to rise further to £6.4m by 2027/28, mainly due to the ending of the £3m per annum lease premium income for Victoria Gate

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Deferred Minimum Revenue Provision accumulated to £595.2m by end-2026/27; acknowledged as temporary accounting mechanism only
findings.detail: The council has deferred £406.5m in MRP through previous Exceptional Financial Support packages. It will defer a further £96.5m in 2025/26 and £92.1m in 2026/27, reaching £595.2m cumulative by end-2026/27. The council and government explicitly acknowledge the Capitalisation Directive mechanism used to defer these costs is temporary only, with deferred MRP attracting additional interest and MRP costs in future years.
findings.matters: Deferred MRP is deferring a liability, not eliminating it. The accumulated £595m represents a future obligation that must eventually be repaid or written off. This creates tail risk in later years (2028+) when deferral arrangements expire and these costs must be faced.
findings.figures: £406.5m deferred as at 31 March 2025; £96.5m in 2025/26; £92.1m in 2026/27; £595.2m cumulative total
findings.quote: As a Capitalisation Directive involves further borrowing, the CD itself attracts additional interest and MRP costs in future years, therefore it can only be a temporary, not permanent, solution.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £500m government debt support carries explicit risk of interest cost escalation if delivery is delayed beyond agreed deadline
findings.detail: Government committed in October 2025 to provide £500m to reduce the council's debt from £2.2bn to £1.7bn, conditional on asset rationalisation progress. The paper explicitly flags that any delay in receipt beyond an agreed deadline will trigger additional interest costs. Given that interest servicing already consumes £62.6m of the 2026/27 budget, timing delays directly threaten budget viability.
findings.matters: Debt support is contingent and time-sensitive. Interest costs scale with delay duration. Asset sales are complex and subject to market conditions; any slippage cascades into budget deficits that the council cannot absorb without further government support.
findings.figures: £500m debt support reducing debt from £2.2bn to £1.7bn forecast; 2026/27 interest payable £62.6m
findings.quote: There is a key risk to be aware of that should the debt support be delayed beyond any agreed deadline, the Council would incur additional interest costs for the duration of any delay.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-001 General Fund Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Council cannot set a balanced budget without £150.2m government Exceptional Financial Support; dependency is structural
findings.detail: Woking issued a Section 114 notice in June 2023 after expenditure exceeded available resources. The 2026/27 budget requires £150.2m in government support via a Capitalisation Directive (£58.1m) and deferred Minimum Revenue Provision (£92.1m). Without this discretionary government support, the council cannot legally balance its budget. This represents complete fiscal dependence on government bailout rather than self-sufficiency.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether the council can meet obligations independently. Government support is discretionary, not automatic, and could change if political priorities shift or the council fails to meet recovery milestones.
findings.figures: £150.2m EFS request; £58.1m via Capitalisation Directive; £92.1m deferred MRP; underlying debt £2.2bn
findings.quote: Clearly, the size and scale of the historic debt at c.£2.2 billion would prevent a legal budget being set for 2026/27 without the continuation of support from Government.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 1 - Woking EFS Request 2026-27 23 Jan 2026
findings.headline: All usable capital receipts and capital grants are fully committed, with general fund balance at minimum needed level
findings.detail: Usable capital receipts of £21.4m and capital grants unapplied of £4.1m are both fully committed. The general fund balance of £6.5m is stated as the minimum balance needed for adequate protection, with £5m of this established as part of the 2023/24 EFS request.

Usable Capital Receipts - £21.4 million is committed to fund the essential elements of the capital programme and reduce general fund debt.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 1 - Woking EFS Request 2026-27 23 Jan 2026
findings.headline: Forensic review of HRA identified £4.5m in past transaction issues requiring General Fund rectification transfer
findings.detail: A completed forensic review of past/legacy HRA transactions resulted in a £4.5m rectification transfer from the General Fund to the HRA. The £4.5m had previously been set aside in an earmarked reserve. While this resolves a material uncertainty, it reveals past HRA accounting or governance issues.

findings.headline: Business-as-usual budget shows increasing deficits of £5.5m (2027/28) and £6.7m (2028/29) even with £2.7m new savings for 2026/27
findings.detail: Despite identifying £2.7m in new savings for 2026/27 (bringing the budget to break-even in that year), the forecast BAU budget envelope shows deficits of £5.5m in 2027/28 and £6.7m in 2028/29, indicating structural underlying budget pressures that persist beyond the support period.

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 1 - Woking EFS Request 2026-27 23 Jan 2026

findings.paper_title: WBC26-008 Appendix 1 - Woking EFS Request 2026-27 23 Jan 2026
findings.headline: Both external auditors will issue disclaimers of opinion on all accounts from 2019/20 through 2024/25
findings.detail: BDO will issue disclaimer of opinion on 2019/20 to 2022/23 accounts; Grant Thornton will issue disclaimer on 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts. This means the auditors cannot give a clean bill of health on any of these years' financial statements.
findings.matters: Disclaimers of opinion indicate the auditors could not obtain sufficient evidence to provide reasonable assurance, which is a fundamental audit weakness affecting credibility of financial position.
