findings.quote: BDO anticipates issuing a disclaimer of opinion on each set of the statement of accounts between 2019/20 and 2022/23... Grant Thornton anticipates issuing a disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 and 2024/25 statement of accounts.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Capital programme severely restricted to essential spending only following Section 114
findings.detail: The Council's capital programme has been dramatically reduced from pre-2023 levels. General Fund capital spending is only £12 million in 2026/27, restricted to essential health/safety works, essential IT, government-specified schemes, and schemes returning revenue savings. No new capital expenditure financed by borrowing is permitted outside the annual budget process.
findings.matters: The restriction on capital spending indicates the council cannot fund infrastructure investment and must defer maintenance, which could lead to service deterioration over time.
findings.figures: General Fund capital 2026/27: £12 million (vs historical levels of c£100m+); total capital programme 2026/27: £30 million
findings.quote: Prudential borrowing has previously been the main source of capital finance in recent years but must be minimised as part of the Improvement and Recovery Plan's objective of reducing the Council's debt. From 2026/27 the reduced capital programme now only utilises prudential borrowing for the housing capital programme.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: HRA financing costs rising as percentage of revenue, threatening housing service sustainability
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account financing costs are increasing as a share of revenues and per dwelling. Costs per dwelling are forecast to rise from £1,731 in 2025/26 to £2,227 by 2028/29. The later years' affordability should be reviewed carefully as part of the forthcoming HRA Business Plan.
findings.matters: Rising HRA financing costs relative to revenues indicate the housing service is becoming less sustainable. Right-to-buy sales reduce the revenue base while debt remains constant, worsening affordability.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs per dwelling: £1,731 (2025/26) rising to £2,227 (2028/29); HRA dwellings forecast to fall from 3,200 to 2,969
findings.quote: If financing costs as a share of HRA revenues or per dwelling rises by more than inflation, that represents a bigger call on limited HRA resources. The affordability of later years should be reviewed carefully as part of the forthcoming HRA Business Plan.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Asset rationalisation programme underway but realisable value far below borrowing cost
findings.detail: The Council is selling assets to repay debt as part of its recovery plan. However, the likely realisable value of investment assets is significantly below the associated borrowing. Historic investment spending was c£1.4 billion, but balance sheet value of the investment property portfolio is c£246 million.
findings.matters: Asset sales will not cover the debt they were incurred to finance, meaning taxpayers bear a loss and debt reduction will be limited by the shortfall.
findings.figures: Historic investment spending c£1.4 billion; investment property portfolio balance sheet value c£246 million (31 March 2025)
findings.quote: The likely realisable value of the Council's investment assets (both on the sole entity balance sheet and those of the Council's wholly owned group companies) is significantly below its investment related borrowing.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Revenue deficits of £58-66 million being capitalised rather than funded from resources
findings.detail: The Council is using capitalisation directions to convert revenue budget shortfalls into capital charges. Revenue shortfalls of £66 million in 2025/26 and £58 million in 2026/27 are being capitalised, increasing the Capital Financing Requirement. This mechanism masks the fact that these deficits must ultimately be funded from borrowing.
findings.matters: Capitalisation of revenue deficits indicates the council cannot balance its budget from revenue sources and is deferring the problem to the future via increased debt.
findings.figures: Revenue shortfall 2025/26: £66 million; 2026/27: £58 million; 2027/28: £59 million
findings.quote: A capitalisation direction is required to meet the overall revenue budget shortfalls estimated £66 million in 2025/26 and £58 million in 2026/27 (as per the final 2026/27 request for Exceptional Financial Support submitted to government).

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Section 114 notice (June 2023) confirmed unaffordable borrowing, inadequate repayment steps, and irrecoverable investments
findings.detail: The June 2023 Section 114 notice clarified that the Council's investment strategy had resulted in unaffordable borrowing, inadequate steps to repay that borrowing, and high values of irrecoverable investments. The Council now operates under Commissioners appointed by the government.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration of financial insolvency. Commissioners effectively manage the council's finances. This represents the most severe governance and financial failure.
findings.figures: Section 114 notice issued June 2023
findings.quote: The Section 114 notice in June 2023 clarified that the Council's Investment Strategy had resulted in unaffordable borrowing; inadequate steps to repay that borrowing; and high values of irrecoverable investments.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Government providing £500 million debt support in 2026/27, but council still requires Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: In October 2025, the Government committed to providing £500 million in 2026/27 to support debt repayment, subject to progress with asset rationalisation. However, even after this reduction, interest costs and MRP will remain at unaffordable levels requiring the Council to seek Exceptional Financial Support into 2026/27.
findings.matters: A lender must understand the council operates under government intervention with a Section 114 notice and Commissioners, indicating loss of financial autonomy and ongoing dependency on external support.
findings.figures: Government debt support: £500 million in 2026/27; revenue shortfall requiring capitalisation direction: £58 million in 2026/27
findings.quote: In October 2025, the Government confirmed its intention to provide an initial tranche of debt support for WBC, totalling £500 million, to support repayment of debt, subject to progress with the asset rationalisation programme. This support will significantly reduce the Council's overall debt burden. However, even after this reduction, the associated interest costs and Minimum Revenue Provision remain at a level that will require the Council to seek Exceptional Financial Support into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision was historically underprovisioned; now corrected and requires government support
findings.detail: The Council historically did not charge Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) on capital loans to third parties, understating the proper charge. An independent review confirmed MRP had been understated. Corrected MRP is forecast at £93 million in 2026/27, but most will be deferred as part of Exceptional Financial Support. Only £1.04 million will be charged in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Historical MRP underprovisioning indicates governance failures and improper financial reporting. The scale of the correction shows how far the council is from affordability without government support.
findings.figures: MRP forecast 2026/27: £93 million; to be deferred as part of Exceptional Financial Support; only £1.04 million charged in 2026/27
findings.quote: In the years leading up to the s114 notice, the Council's MRP was very low in relation to its CFR due to the previous (incorrect) policy of not charging MRP on capital loans to third parties. An independent review by Worth Technical Accounting Solutions confirmed that MRP had been understated.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Commercial investment strategy failed — Thameswey and Victoria Square cannot generate expected cashflows
findings.detail: The Council invested heavily in its own companies (Thameswey Group and Victoria Square Woking Limited) expecting them to generate interest income to cover borrowing costs. Since 2023, these investments have not been able to deliver the required cashflows without ongoing injections of Council cash. Interest income from these companies has been suspended since 2023/24.
findings.matters: The entire investment strategy relied on these companies generating returns; their failure is core to understanding why the council became unable to service its debt.
findings.figures: Historic expenditure on share and loan acquisition c£1.4 billion; investment property portfolio and held for sale assets c£246 million at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: In 2023 it became clear that the Council's commercial investments (Thameswey group of companies and Victoria Square Woking Limited) would not able to deliver the cashflows to meet loan repayments to the Council without further ongoing injections of Council cash via the loans' revolving credit facility. Interest income due to the Council as lender from the Council's commercial companies has been suspended since 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex I Capital Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Council debt of £2.2 billion is the highest per capita of any English authority
findings.detail: As of 31 December 2025, Woking has approximately £2.2 billion of debt, with debt per head of population of approximately £20,000 — described as the highest debt per head of any authority in England. This level of debt is unaffordable, with interest due alone far exceeding the Council's total revenue resources.
findings.matters: A lender assessing risk needs to understand the scale of the debt burden and why it became unaffordable despite initial investment strategy.
findings.figures: c£2.2 billion of debt (31 December 2025); debt per head c£20,000; core revenue resources from Council tax and business rates of less than £20 million
findings.quote: the council has c£2.2 billion of debt (31 December 2025). The Council's debt per head of population - c£20,000 - is the highest debt per head of any authority in England.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Woking Backstop ISA260 Reporting to TCWG 2324 final
findings.headline: Auditor unable to assess going concern due to audit disclaimer
findings.detail: Because Grant Thornton has issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements, they are unable to reach any conclusion on the appropriateness of going concern assumptions. This leaves a material gap in assurance about the council's ability to continue operations.
findings.matters: Going concern assessment is critical to financial reporting credibility. The inability to assess it, combined with the Section 114 notice and financial distress indicators, leaves significant uncertainty about whether the council can continue to operate and meet its obligations.
findings.figures: No specific figures; going concern assessment withheld
findings.quote: As we have been unable to form an opinion on the financial statements, we are unable to draw a conclusion in this area.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Woking Backstop ISA260 Reporting to TCWG 2324 final
findings.headline: Multiple audit findings including incorrect General Fund to HRA charges, procurement weaknesses, and fire safety non-compliance
findings.detail: Value for Money findings identified historic incorrect charges from the General Fund to the HRA, weakness in procurement and contract management, weaknesses in commercial activities and subsidiary monitoring, and delays in remedial actions from fire risk assessments resulting in a Regulatory Notice in December 2023 for breach of the Home Standard.
findings.matters: These findings indicate systematic control weaknesses and regulatory breaches. Incorrect inter-fund charges mask true financial position, procurement weaknesses expose the council to fraud risk, and fire safety breaches represent an unresolved health and safety liability.
findings.figures: Fire safety Regulatory Notice issued December 2023
findings.quote: Historic incorrect charges from the General Fund to the HRA. Weakness in arrangements in procurement and contract management. Weaknesses in Council's commercial activities including monitoring and divesting from the Council's subsidiaries. Delays in remedial actions from fire risk assessments resulting in a Regulatory Notice in December 2023 for breach of the Home Standard.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Woking Backstop ISA260 Reporting to TCWG 2324 final
findings.headline: Public Interest Report issued in November 2024 on financial sustainability and governance with five statutory recommendations
findings.detail: Grant Thornton issued a Public Interest Report in November 2024 specifically regarding arrangements for financial sustainability and governance at Woking. The report included five statutory recommendations; three have since been closed but two remain as key recommendations, indicating ongoing concerns.
findings.matters: A Public Interest Report is a serious regulatory action signalling matters of public concern. Ongoing unresolved key recommendations indicate that governance weaknesses remain unaddressed.
findings.figures: Five statutory recommendations issued; three closed, two downgraded to key recommendations as of 28 January 2026
findings.quote: We issued a report in the Public Interest with regard to arrangements for financial sustainability and governance at Woking Borough Council in November 2024. Our Public Interest Report included five statutory recommendations. We have since closed three of the statutory recommendations and downgrade the remaining two to key recommendations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Woking Backstop ISA260 Reporting to TCWG 2324 final
findings.headline: Section 114 notice issued due to historic unaffordable debt levels and poor financial position
findings.detail: The Value for Money findings explicitly cite the council's financial position and historic unaffordable levels of debt as having led to the issue of a Section 114 notice. A Section 114 notice signals that the s151 officer believes the council cannot afford its spending commitments.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a statutory warning that the council is effectively insolvent or unable to set a balanced budget. This is the most serious financial governance action available and directly affects a lender's assessment of the council's viability.
findings.figures: Section 114 notice issued (no date given in this document)
findings.quote: The Council's financial position and historic unaffordable levels of debt leading to the issue of the Section 114 notice.

findings.paper_title: Appendix D - Woking Backstop ISA260 Reporting to TCWG 2324 final
findings.headline: 2023/24 audit opinion disclaimed due to inability to obtain sufficient evidence by statutory deadline
findings.detail: Grant Thornton was unable to complete the 2023/24 audit by the 28 February 2025 backstop date because prior year audits (up to 2022/23) had not been disclaimed. This means they cannot form any audit opinion on the financial statements, issuing instead a disclaimer. The auditor concludes that undetected misstatements could be both material and pervasive.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means there is no independent verification of the council's financial statements, leaving material misstatement undetected. This is a severe credibility blow for financial reporting and makes it impossible for a lender to rely on the accounts.
findings.figures: Backstop date 28 February 2025; accounts published 16 January 2025
findings.quote: We have concluded that the possible effects on the financial statements of undetected misstatements arising from this matter could be both material and pervasive. We have therefore issued a disclaimer of opinion on the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-019 PART I Investment Debt Repayment and Standstill for the ThamesWey Group 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.headline: Minimal debt recovery with only £2m cash sweep against unquantified total debt
findings.detail: The council's only immediate cash recovery mechanism is a £2m cash sweep for the period to end December 2025. This is presented as contributing 'in principle' to debt reduction but represents minimal recovery against the substantial unsecured debt and interest accruing during the standstill.
findings.matters: The council is deferring debt service indefinitely while nominal debt grows through accrued interest, recovering minimal cash, which delays resolution of the underlying financial problem and extends the period of dependency on government support.
findings.figures: £2,000,000 cash sweep to end December 2025; next sweep assessment to end March 2026
findings.quote: The Group proposed a debt sweep of £2,000,000 for the period to the end of December 2025. The Council, through the Section 151 officer who was delegated authority in July, has accepted

findings.paper_title: EXE26-019 PART I Investment Debt Repayment and Standstill for the ThamesWey Group 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.headline: Council dependent on central government Exceptional Financial Support to confirm its own debt standstill
findings.detail: The council cannot formally confirm the 2026/27 standstill until Exceptional Financial Support from central government is confirmed. The council is itself in formal intervention (Section 114 notice issued May 2023) and the standstill approval is contingent on continued central government support, creating circular dependency.
findings.matters: A council borrowing capacity and debt servicing is contingent on government support that is conditional on council performance, creating risk that support could be withdrawn and debt service obligations could become unaffordable.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support (2025/26 announced February 2025; 2026/27 timing uncertain)
findings.quote: The Council cannot formally confirm a debt standstill position for 2026/27 until it has confirmed Exceptional Financial Support from central government for the 2026/27 financial year

findings.paper_title: EXE26-019 PART I Investment Debt Repayment and Standstill for the ThamesWey Group 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.headline: Asset impairment is substantial with unsecured debt exceeding asset value
findings.detail: The council holds loans to ThamesWey companies where fixed asset values are less than liabilities. The report identifies a substantial gap between asset values and debt, which would crystallize as unsecured loss if the companies entered administration.
findings.matters: This indicates the council has lent beyond recoverable asset value, creating real losses that will eventually crystallize as budget pressure or impact on council finances.
findings.figures: Asset value less than liabilities; unsecured debt value described as 'substantial' with no quantification
findings.quote: the value of the fixed assets of the group are less than their liabilities

findings.paper_title: EXE26-019 PART I Investment Debt Repayment and Standstill for the ThamesWey Group 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.headline: Companies are insolvent and dependent on standstill to avoid administration
findings.detail: The ThamesWey companies cannot service their debt to Woking Council from operations. The council's financial advisor Interpath found that if debt charges were applied at contracted levels, the companies would become cash flow insolvent immediately, forcing directors to enter administration. The standstill agreement is required to keep the companies solvent and trading.
findings.matters: A council that cannot recover its loans and is managing insolvency rather than resolution presents material credit risk to lenders, particularly when dependent on central government support.
findings.figures: £2,000,000 cash sweep for period to end December 2025
findings.quote: if debt charges are applied at the levels agreed before the current investment debt standstill the group of companies would become cash flow insolvent in the very near term. This would precipitate a formal insolvency process

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Capital programme suspended in September 2023 and reduced for 2024-25
findings.detail: Due to the Council's debt position and need to minimise capital expenditure, the capital programme was suspended in September 2023 and then reduced for 2024-25. Current General Fund capital programme is under £9m, with focus restricted to Council Housing for health, safety and decent homes compliance.
findings.matters: A suspended and severely reduced capital programme indicates financial stress and constrained investment capacity, with potential service delivery implications.
findings.figures: General Fund capital programme under £9m; programme suspended September 2023
findings.quote: Due to the Council's debt position and the need to minimise capital expenditure, the previous capital programme was suspended in September 2023 and the programme for 2024/25 has been reduced.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Revenue recognition testing on fees and charges left incomplete with 89 unresolved queries
findings.detail: The auditor selected 89 items of fees and charges income for testing but could not complete the sample due to unresolved queries. This revenue stream was assessed as high-risk for fraud due to nature and susceptibility to manipulation.
findings.matters: Incomplete testing on a high-risk revenue area leaves a material earnings component unverified and creates audit uncertainty about income quality.
findings.figures: 89 items selected for testing; majority had unresolved queries
findings.quote: Our sample testing of fees and charges was not completed. There were unresolved queries for the majority of the 89 items selected for testing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Asset valuations show material errors including £595k overstatement and £17.8m leisure centre understatement
findings.detail: The Council's fixed asset register does not reconcile with valuation reports, revealing an overstatement of £595k. Additionally, £49.4m of land and buildings that should have been revalued on a rolling programme were not, and leisure centre valuations were understated by £17.8m due to a disagreement with the external valuer over depreciable amounts.
findings.matters: Asset valuations drive both the balance sheet size and capital decision-making; material errors here indicate the Council's financial position is not accurately reported.
findings.figures: £595k overstatement; £49,414k of assets not revalued; £17,806k leisure centre understatement
findings.quote: Our testing revealed an overstatement of £595k due to the differences between the Fixed Asset Register and Valuation Reports. We noted £49,414k of other land and buildings that should have been revalued in 2024/25 that have not been subject to valuation. An understatement of £17,806k relating to the valuation of leisure centres was identified.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Journal posting controls lack approval requirement for senior personnel
findings.detail: Senior finance staff can post journal entries without requiring approval, creating an uncontrolled pathway for errors or fraud at year-end when many adjusting journals are posted (revaluations, accruals, PPE movements). The auditor tested 53 high-value or unusual journals and could not clear 34.
findings.matters: Weak journal controls are a classic audit finding that enables misstatement; combined with capacity issues, this increases the risk of undetected error in the financial statements.
findings.figures: 53 journals selected for testing; 34 could not be cleared as at 5 January 2026
findings.quote: Senior personnel are theoretically able to post journal entries. Without the approval process we consider there is an increased risk of undetected fraud or error.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in Value for Money arrangements identified
findings.detail: The auditor is not satisfied that Woking Borough Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. Weaknesses span the Council's overall arrangements, financial sustainability, and governance.
findings.matters: VFM weaknesses indicate the Council cannot reliably demonstrate prudent use of funds or financial sustainability, increasing risk for any lender.
findings.figures: Full VFM assessment to be published in separate Auditor's Annual Report
findings.quote: We identified significant weaknesses in the Council's arrangements so are not satisfied that the Council has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Finance team capacity insufficient to meet audit demands
findings.detail: The Council struggled throughout the audit to provide timely evidence, responses to queries, and supporting documentation. The auditor notes that delays in providing evidence and responding to follow-up queries prevented completion of testing, and the Council has acknowledged this is a capacity issue needing resolution.
findings.matters: A finance team without sufficient capacity to support an audit cannot reliably produce financial reporting or manage financial controls, raising questions about day-to-day financial stewardship.
findings.figures: Just over 50% of audit samples cleared; significant delays in providing evidence
findings.quote: The Council needs to improve its timeliness in providing audit evidence and responses to audit queries to enable a full audit to be completed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: No assurance over opening balances or closing reserve positions
findings.detail: Four years of disclaimed audits prior to 2024-25 mean the auditor has no verified starting point for reserves or opening balances. This uncertainty cascades through the entire financial statement, preventing the auditor from verifying the year-end reserve position.
findings.matters: Reserves are the Council's financial shock absorber; without assurance on them, both the starting position and the ability to manage unexpected pressures are unknown.
findings.figures: No baseline verification of opening balances or closing reserves for 2024-25
findings.quote: As a result, for 2024/25: we have no assurance over the opening balances for 2024/25; no assurance over the closing reserves balance also due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - WBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Auditor unable to issue unmodified opinion on 2024-25 financial statements
findings.detail: Grant Thornton cannot provide assurance over opening balances and closing reserves, and has only completed testing on 50% of samples by the backstop date. The Council is moving to a unitary while trying to rebuild audit assurance, compressing the timeline further.
findings.matters: An unqualified audit opinion is essential for accessing lending markets; a disclaimer opinion signals deep uncertainty about financial position and governance.
findings.figures: 50% of samples cleared by 31 December 2025; backstop deadline 27 February 2026
findings.quote: Owing to the challenges of undertaking an audit where the previous years' audits were subject to backstop-related disclaimed audit opinions, we have been unable to undertake sufficient work to support an unmodified audit opinion in advance of the backstop date of 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: A cladding failure on the Victoria Square hotel threatens to reduce proceeds from a major asset scheduled for sale.
findings.detail: The council is pursuing a three-year divestment programme for assets including the hotel (part of Victoria Square's £134m asset base). Cladding remediation requirements have emerged as an unexpected cost that will reduce net sale proceeds and complicate the disposal timeline.
findings.matters: This is a concrete example of hidden costs on the commercial portfolio that reduce cash available for debt repayment and demonstrate execution risk in the divestment plan.
findings.figures: Victoria Square fixed assets £134m, cladding remediation now required before sale
findings.quote: Issues which may have a potentially material impact on divestment values include the recent cladding failure on the Victoria Square Woking Limited hotel

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: The commercial property portfolio is adding to General Fund losses rather than generating net income.
findings.detail: Over 60 commercial assets (shopping centres, office buildings, industrial estates) generate rental income insufficient to cover financing costs, service charges, and business rates. The impact of void management and rising landlord costs is creating ongoing losses to the General Fund budget.
findings.matters: These assets are liabilities, not revenue generators. They consume council resources and reduce financial flexibility while their sale is essential to the debt reduction plan.
findings.figures: £247m portfolio valuation, insufficient rental income to service financing and holding costs
findings.quote: Whilst the assets contribute rental income to the Council's budget, this is currently insufficient to service financing and holding costs. The operational impact of managing the loss of income from voids alongside the associated increase in costs to the landlord (the Council) for service charges and business rates has had a significant impact on the General Fund

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: The two main investment companies cannot service their £46m annual interest bill from operations and rely on a debt standstill.
findings.detail: Thameswey and Victoria Square Woking Limited are operationally profitable (EBITDA positive) but insufficient to cover interest and principal. Interest accrual is suspended subject to government support through the Capitalisation Direction, and this standstill has been extended into 2026/27.
findings.matters: The council has no cash flow from its £571m net loan book (after impairments). The indefinite standstill shows these assets cannot generate returns and depend on government forbearance.
findings.figures: £46m annual suspended interest, £413.6m Thameswey loans at fair value, £145.6m Victoria Square loans at fair value
findings.quote: The two groups of companies make positive earnings before interest payments, taxation, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) but they are not earning enough to meet their full interest and principal payment liabilities. The interest due to the Council from the Thameswey group of companies and Victoria Square Woking Limited is c£46 million per annum

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Between £1.2bn and £1.4bn of the council's debt is not backed by realisable assets.
findings.detail: The council borrowed far beyond the value of the assets purchased. Loans to companies were impaired by £818m and share investments by £33m, reflecting the fundamental mismatch between debt and asset values. This unsecured portion cannot be recovered through asset sales.
findings.matters: This reveals the debt cannot be repaid from asset sales alone—any repayment depends on government debt forgiveness or restructuring, not commercial performance.
findings.figures: £1.2-1.4bn unsecured of £1.8bn total, £818m loan impairments, £33m share impairments
findings.quote: It is estimated that between £1.2 billion and £1.4 billion of the Council's debt is not backed by realisable assets

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Woking has the highest debt per head of any council in England and requires ongoing government Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: The council holds c£1.8bn in investments financed by borrowing, with total debt far exceeding asset values. It cannot set its annual budget without government support, and this will continue to be required even after the £500m debt relief in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Lenders face a council whose basic budget viability depends entirely on continued government intervention rather than operational sustainability.
findings.figures: £1.8bn total group investments, highest debt per head in UK
findings.quote: The Council currently has the highest debt per head of population of any local authority in the UK with total group investments of c£1.8 billion ... the Council requires Exceptional Financial Support from government to be able to set its annual budget and Council Tax

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex II Investment Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Even after £500m government debt relief and total asset disposal, Woking faces a persistent structural deficit.
findings.detail: The council's debt model shows that even if all commercial assets and properties were fully disposed of, the General Fund would face a significant structural deficit driven largely by interest and Minimum Revenue Provision charges. This means the fundamental affordability problem extends beyond the commercial portfolio.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand this is not a portfolio problem that can be solved by asset sales—the council has a structural budget problem that will persist regardless of divestment success.
findings.figures: £500m debt relief in 2026/27, borrowing to reduce to around £1.7bn from £2.2bn
findings.quote: even if all commercial assets (including the commercial property portfolio and company holdings) were fully disposed of, the General Fund would continue to face a significant structural deficit largely driven by debt interest and Minimum Revenue Provision costs

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft)
findings.headline: PWLB loan premiums create a structural barrier to efficient debt repayment; council using internal borrowing as workaround
findings.detail: PWLB early repayment penalties (premiums or discounts) make actual debt repayment uneconomical on some loans. Council is currently using capital receipts for internal borrowing instead of debt repayment, pending government review of PWLB mechanics. This extends the effective life of debt while maintaining the appearance of CFR reduction.
findings.matters: The council's debt burden may persist longer than the numbers suggest; the distinction between CFR reduction and actual debt repayment matters for long-term sustainability.
findings.figures: Discount rate references to PWLB annuity rates (not numerically specified in figures)
findings.quote: The premium (or discount) payment required on PWLB loans will be calculated as part of any debt charge savings as it can be a disincentive to actual debt repayment so this should NOT be used in a decision on sale

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft)
findings.headline: Council is operating under government Commissioners with restricted autonomy over capital receipt deployment
findings.detail: Multiple references to 'Council's Commissioners' indicate the council is under government intervention. Commissioners must formally approve any exception to the default policy of applying all General Fund capital receipts to debt reduction.
findings.matters: Lenders should understand the council is in special measures and cannot freely redeploy capital receipts for transformation spending or other priorities without external approval.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Any exceptions should be agreed by the Council's Commissioners and any other relevant formal approval required.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft)
findings.headline: Council is disposing of most or all of its investment portfolio to reduce debt levels
findings.detail: The investment portfolio is under comprehensive review with the explicit aim of disposing of most or all assets to reduce council debt. This is part of the Commercial workstream of the Improvement and Recovery Plan, overseen by the Commercial and Finance Governance Board.
findings.matters: Loss of investment income reduces revenue capacity; forced asset sales may occur at unfavourable prices if disposals are urgent; liquidation risk if portfolio cannot be sold.
findings.figures: Portfolio extent not quantified in this appendix
findings.quote: The Council's investment portfolio is currently under comprehensive review with a view to disposing of most or all of them in order to reduce the Council's debt.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft)
findings.headline: £500 million government debt support for 2026/27 is conditional on successful completion of the asset rationalisation plan
findings.detail: Government has committed to £500m debt support but explicitly links it to progress on asset disposals. If the council fails to dispose of assets as planned, this support may not be released. This creates execution risk: asset disposal failures would eliminate the funding solution for the MRP gap.
findings.matters: Lenders must assess the probability that asset disposals will succeed and funding will not be withdrawn mid-year.
findings.figures: £500m debt support committed
findings.quote: Government have committed to £500 million debt support in 2026/27 subject to progress with the asset rationalisation plan.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices (Draft)
findings.headline: Council's £95 million Minimum Revenue Provision for 2026/27 is unaffordable and must be deferred via government support
findings.detail: The calculated MRP is £95m, but the council can only afford £1.042m as 'business as usual' provision. The £93.96m balance is being deferred through an application for government Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) pending a long-term solution. This fundamentally means the council cannot service its debt at the calculated prudent level.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's debt servicing capacity is dependent on government bailout support and whether that support will materialise if asset disposals fail.
findings.figures: Calculated MRP £95m; affordable level £1.042m (2025/26 £8m); deferred £93.96m
findings.quote: The Council's estimated MRP for 2026/27 – calculated based on the policy above - is £95 million. The Council's 2026/27 MRP as calculated is unaffordable and cannot be met in full by the Council.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Council borrowing requires government approval at every stage; all new borrowing subject to regular MHCLG review meetings
findings.detail: As the council is in intervention and receiving Exceptional Financial Support, specific conditions restrict borrowing activity including regular reporting of cash flow position and advance approval for any borrowing. All borrowing will be with PWLB. Regular meetings with MHCLG review and agree the council's borrowing needs before PWLB loans are drawn down.
findings.matters: Loss of borrowing autonomy signals deep mistrust of council financial management; this external control will constrain operational flexibility and introduces execution risk around timing of necessary borrowing
findings.figures: All borrowing subject to MHCLG advance approval; regular review meetings required
findings.quote: Due to the scale of the debt held these will include regular reporting of the cash flow position and advance approval for any borrowing required... Regular meetings with MHCLG review and agree the Council's borrowing needs.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Mandatory asset rationalisation plan required; capital receipts must be used for debt reduction, not service investment
findings.detail: As part of the intervention, the council is required to reduce the level of assets held to reduce outstanding debt. A key principle is that all proceeds from sale of General Fund assets (including company assets) will be applied to reduce debt or finance existing capital commitments, not fund additional expenditure. Progress is being overseen jointly with Commissioners.
findings.matters: Forced asset sales at potentially distressed valuations; the council cannot reinvest proceeds, limiting its ability to generate income or maintain service provision; this is a long-term structural weakness
findings.figures: Asset Rationalisation Plan underway; all proceeds presumed to reduce debt or finance existing commitments
findings.quote: The key principle is that all proceeds from the sale of General Fund assets (including those from the Council's companies), will be presumed to be used to reduce debt or finance existing capital commitments, rather than fund additional expenditure.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: A 1 percent rise in interest rates would cost the council £5 million in 2026-27; the council is extremely vulnerable to rate changes
findings.detail: The strategy identifies that a 1% rise in interest rates would create a general fund impact of £5 million in 2026-27. The council holds an extremely high level of loan debt and is 'very vulnerable to interest rate changes'. Short-term borrowing limits are set at 40% of debt to manage this risk.
findings.matters: Interest rate sensitivity is high due to debt scale; with short-term borrowing needed for refinancing, the council faces material upside risk to financing costs if rates rise contrary to current forecasts
findings.figures: General Fund impact of 1% rise in interest rates: £5 million in 2026-27; 40% maximum short-term and variable rate debt limit
findings.quote: This Council with an extremely high level of loan debt is very vulnerable to interest rate changes.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Reliance on £500 million government debt relief; without it the council cannot achieve financial sustainability
findings.detail: The government has committed to providing £500 million of debt support. This is a core assumption in the council's financial forecasts. The strategy states 'further support is expected to be required in future, as the Council is unable to meet all remaining borrowing liabilities and associated debt-charge costs.' Payment date and detailed mechanism remain unconfirmed.
findings.matters: The entire financial recovery plan depends on government debt relief that has not been finalised; without it, the council has no path to sustainability; this creates significant execution risk
findings.figures: £500m government debt support committed; full details and payment date not yet confirmed
findings.quote: As previously mentioned, the Government has committed to providing £500m of debt support. The payment date and full details of the mechanism have not yet been confirmed.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Council has systematically understated Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP), with £406.5 million backlog already deferred
findings.detail: An independent external review confirmed the council has systematically understated its MRP due to a policy of not charging MRP on loans to companies. Backlog MRP of £406.5 million has been included in previous Exceptional Financial Support packages, with a further £96.5m deferred in 2025-26. For 2026-27, the council is requesting to charge only £1.045 million 'business as usual' MRP with £92m deferred.
findings.matters: MRP deferral is a form of debt restructuring that pushes repayment into the future; the magnitude (£406.5m backlog plus ongoing deferrals) shows the council cannot sustain proper debt repayment from operations
findings.figures: Backlog MRP £406.5m; 2025-26 additional MRP deferred £96.5m; 2026-27 requested 'business as usual' MRP £1.045m with £92m deferred
findings.quote: This review confirmed the Council, due predominantly to the policy of not charging MRP on the loans to companies, has systematically understated its MRP. Backlog MRP included in previous Exceptional Financial Support packages totalled £406.5 million. In 2025/26, a further £96.5m MRP is expected to be deferred within the current EFS package.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Interest income from wholly-owned companies (ThamesWey and VSWL) has been suspended entirely
findings.detail: The council previously received interest income from ThamesWey and VSWL, wholly-owned commercial companies. This interest is now zero due to suspension. The loss of these revenues is the main driver of the need for a Capitalisation Directive to cover revenue expenditure.
findings.matters: Complete suspension of company dividend/interest income shows failed commercial strategy; the council relied on commercial returns to fund operations and borrowing costs, creating a structural vulnerability
findings.figures: Interest from ThamesWey and VSWL: £0k for all forecast years (2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29)
findings.quote: The main element of the Capitalisation Directive will be to cover the loss of revenues arising from the suspension of interest previously paid by the wholly owned companies.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Gross annual interest costs of £68.6 million with council unable to sustain this burden even with £500m government debt support
findings.detail: The council faces gross interest payable of £68.6 million in 2026-27, with General Fund gross financing costs of £63.7 million. The strategy explicitly states this interest burden is 'far higher than the Council is able to sustain even with the £500m debt support confirmed by Government' and that further support is expected to be required in future.
findings.matters: This represents an unsustainable structural deficit that cannot be resolved through operational efficiency; the council is explicitly stating that even with £500m debt relief, borrowing costs remain unaffordable
findings.figures: Gross interest payable £68,572k; General Fund financing costs £63,651k for 2026-27
findings.quote: Given the suspension of interest income from the Group Company investments, this interest burden is far higher than the Council is able to sustain even with the £500m debt support confirmed by Government.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Council must borrow £444 million in 2026-27, mainly to refinance £357 million of maturing loans
findings.detail: The council faces a borrowing requirement of £444 million in 2026-27, consisting of £357 million of existing loans maturing that need to be reborrowed plus an £87 million increase in new loan debt. The increase is driven by a Capitalisation Directive to cover revenue expenditure until the council reaches a sustainable financial position.
findings.matters: Massive refinancing needs combined with structural revenue deficits create ongoing dependency on capital markets and government support; maturity profile shows significant refinancing risk
findings.figures: £444m total borrowing requirement; £357m maturing loans; £87m increase in loan debt; £60m capitalisation directive for revenue shortfall
findings.quote: The Council's borrowing requirement in paragraph 4 above shows a borrowing requirement of £444 million for 2026/27 mainly replacing maturing loans as well as supporting some limited capital expenditure.

findings.paper_title: EXE26-004 Annex III Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 (Draft)
findings.headline: Section 114 notice issued in June 2023 due to extremely high loan debt and failed commercial company investments
findings.detail: The council issued a Section 114 notice (formal notice of financial distress) in June 2023 because of a combination of very high loan debt and reliance on failed high-value investments in commercial companies to fund borrowing costs. These remain the underpinning causes of the council's financial difficulties.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is the most serious financial distress signal in local government and signals fundamental structural problems that take years to resolve
findings.figures: Section 114 notice issued June 2023
findings.quote: The Council's financial difficulties (underpinning the issuing of a Section 114 notice in June 2023) relate to the extremely high level of the Council's loan debt combined with the Council's reliance on failed high value investments in the commercial companies to fund the borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: EXE25-096 Housing Revenue Account Forensic Review
findings.headline: Ongoing risks with ThamesWey subsidiary: energy pricing requires benchmarking; solar panel lease confirmed legally unenforceable
findings.detail: The Phase Two review recommends comprehensive benchmarking of ThamesWey Energy Limited's power rates against external providers to ensure value for money, and review of Energy Service Charge payments for obsolete assets to identify potential overpayment recovery. Legal advice confirms the draft solar panel lease with ThamesWey is not binding because essential terms were not completed, suggesting weak contract management over subsidiary arrangements.
findings.matters: Lenders view uncontrolled related-party pricing and legally deficient agreements as high-risk areas; weak subsidiary oversight undermines financial sustainability and indicates potential for unexpected costs.
findings.figures: Benchmarking exercise in progress; solar lease identified as unenforceable
findings.quote: The KC advice has subsequently confirmed that the draft lease between the Council and ThamesWey for solar panels is not binding on the Council, because essential terms were not completed or agreed.

findings.paper_title: EXE25-096 Housing Revenue Account Forensic Review
findings.headline: Yellow Phase capital disposal paused indefinitely; £316k undervaluation identified and valuation methodology found flawed
findings.detail: Errors in the Debt Supportable Workbook understate the Yellow Phase land transfer value by approximately £316k. The valuation methodology was inappropriate, based on pre-demolition property status rather than actual land condition. The transfer has been paused to prevent loss. A revised Executive report will present corrected debt values and transparent explanation of the valuation basis in October 2025.
findings.matters: Delayed capital disposals reduce cash generation and compromise financial planning; valuation errors compound governance concerns and create risk of further unexpected losses on asset transfers.
findings.figures: £316,049 identified undervaluation
findings.quote: These errors resulted in an understatement of approximately £316,049 of the land transfer value, creating a risk that the land could be transferred at a greater undervalue than planned.

findings.paper_title: EXE25-096 Housing Revenue Account Forensic Review
findings.headline: Forensic review identifies systemic audit weaknesses: many transactions lacked supporting evidence, no formal agreements with ThamesWey, poor planning caused substantial losses
findings.detail: The forensic review found many HRA transactions lacked adequate supporting evidence for key details like purchase prices and costs, formal agreements were absent for ThamesWey transactions including subsidy arrangements, and inadequate planning for rehousing led to significant rental losses, security costs, and unnecessary disturbance payments on retained properties. These control environment failures allowed £4m+ in improper charges to accumulate over time.
findings.matters: Systematic control weaknesses indicate elevated risk of further unidentified issues in financial statements; lenders assess governance quality as an indicator of financial reporting reliability and management competence.
findings.figures: £316,049 debt calculation understatement identified, losses from planning failures described as 'significant' but total amount not separately itemised
findings.quote: A significant number of transactions were found to lack adequate supporting evidence, making it difficult to substantiate key details such as the accuracy of purchase prices and incidental costs.

findings.paper_title: EXE25-096 Housing Revenue Account Forensic Review
findings.headline: General Fund transfer of £4.49m required to correct HRA charges; legacy risk reserve depletes from £6.2m to £1.6m
findings.detail: The forensic review identified £4.07m in transactions incorrectly charged to the HRA, primarily £3.84m for planning and design work transferred to ThamesWey without payment, and £0.23m for pub demolition. Including interest, the General Fund must transfer £4.49m to the HRA to correct these charges. This exhausts most of the legacy risk reserve, leaving only £1.6m remaining and significantly limiting the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Lenders assess reserve adequacy as a key credit indicator; material reserve depletion to cover past errors signals reduced capacity to manage future challenges and cash flow volatility.
findings.figures: £3,841,106 (design work), £231,924 (pub), total transfer £4,490,582, General Fund reserve reduces from £6,200,000 to £1,627,616
findings.quote: The proposed transfer from the General Fund to the HRA including interest totals £4,490,582, which can be funded by an existing General Fund legacy risk reserve.

news_drafts.headline: Council remains under government commissioners' oversight with no autonomous borrowing authority
news_drafts.lead: Lenders should understand the council operates under statutory constraints with external governance oversight, limiting management autonomy in financial decision-making and borrowing strategy.

news_drafts.headline: Total borrowing increased to £2,185.4m despite debt reduction plan and asset disposals
news_drafts.lead: Net debt increase contradicts the narrative of debt reduction and suggests the restructuring has not yet achieved primary trajectory improvement. The CD usage for revenue is outpacing asset sale proceeds.

news_drafts.headline: Revenue expenditure continues to be funded through Capitalisation Direction due to structural deficit
news_drafts.lead: This is a direct indicator of ongoing structural revenue deficit; the council remains dependent on special borrowing permissions to fund day-to-day expenditure, not just capital investment. This is the core condition that triggered the section 114 notice.
